The new edition also contains five colorful illustrations by artist Nate Christopherson. The book quickly became a hit and appeared on the bestseller lists of The New York Times , The Washington Post , and Los Angeles Times . Literary Hub also gave the book the epithet of “Best Essay Collection of the Decade”, while The Washington Post and Minneapolis Star Tribune also put it on their lists for holiday gift recommendations. Book Riot and Food Tank also highly recommended it. Braiding Sweetgrass won the 2014 Sigurd F. Olson Nature Writing Award, given in honor of the literary legacy of Sigurd F. Olson to the best environmental writings in adult nonfiction and children’s literature. Despite its success, Braiding Sweetgrass did not have a large-scale marketing campaign. Instead, it became popular through “word of mouth” and recommendations from one reader to the other. According to the author, this may be because the time is ripe for the message when inequalities and injustices have become so apparent. Kimmerer wrote the first draft of the book in purple ink on long yellow legal pads, sitting outside in nature and observing small things in the natural world that can act as microcosms for great ideas. The name, Braiding Sweetgrass , is a metaphor referring to the fact that the stories told in the book are made up of three strands: the traditional indigenous perspective about environment, scientific knowledge about plants, and the beauty of the knowledge that plants themselves hold and can teach those who want to learn. The book is supposed to be a braid of stories using three different ways of defining our relationship with the natural world. Braiding Sweetgrass has a rating of 4.58 on Goodreads and 4.8 on Amazon. The book has been praised for being a profoundly important work. The few criticisms of the book state that the stories run together and are often repetitive, and the author’s presentation of the subject is completely one-sided, not taking into account the social problems of indigenous or traditional societies. However, the book remains popular, and the author has been commended on her take on this complicated subject. Discussion Questions question 1 In the first chapter, Kimmerer compares the Potawatomi story of the Skywoman to the Christian story of Eve and points out how their relationships to the earth vary. What do these stories about the first woman in these different cultures tell about them and their attitude about women? What is the lesson they share about human’s relationship with nature? Compare and discuss. question 2 Kimmerer gives the example of Evon Peter, who claimed he was raised by a river. In the same vein, Kimmerer herself claims to be raised by strawberries. Which part of nature would you consider you were raised by, and why? Describe what role nature has played in your life and how it has affected the person you have become today. question 3 Kimmerer talks about the differing concepts of private property economy and a gift economy. In the former, a gift is just a gift and is free to be used or not by the recipient. In a gift economy, a gift is used to build relationships and must be rooted in reciprocity. She applies this to land ownership. What else can these concepts be applied to? Discuss gifts and their cultural implications in different cultures. question 4 Kimmerer started taking classes in her native language, Potawatomi. There are only nine speakers left who speak it fluently. What do you think can be done to revive these almost-lost languages? How much effort should the government put into reparations and revitalizing these lost languages? Discuss how the US government and the settler community (European immigrants in the Americas) can make reparations for the loss of culture and language for the Native Americans. question 5 Kimmerer’s daughter refused to stand up for the American Pledge of Allegiance in her school. What do you think this pledge denotes, and why do you think she was refusing to acknowledge this? Can we truly be global citizens if we put our own country first? question 6 Kimmerer shares different stories and legends of the Potawatomi with readers. Which one of these did you like the most, and why? In what way does this specific story resonate with your own life? question 7 The author explains the concept of Honorable Harvest, which dictates to take only what you need and use everything you take. How does this differ from the practices in our modern-day society? How would it be possible for us to practice honorable harvest today? question 8 Kimmerer points out that the settlers behave like they are planning to go back to their homeland even after several generations. She says that the best way for them to blend in is to be naturalized and become one with the land. How do you think white people in the US can do this? How does this advice work for the next wave of immigrants in the US from Asia, Africa, and South America? question 9 On one of her college field trips, Kimmerer raised the question of how or even whether they could give back to nature in return for her gifts. Her students arrived at a number of interesting answers. What is your opinion about this? question 10 The book is all about the interactions between humans and their environment. The author gives her own example of her special relationship with certain plants. Is there a plant in your environment with which you feel a special relationship? Which one is it, and why do you feel this way about it? If not, why? Would your life be enriched with such a special relationship with a plant?
